query: I am interested in the thermal stability and atomic diffusion behavior of nearly equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HENA) composed of five transition metals. What are the fundamental factors governing their structural evolution at elevated temperatures, and how does their behavior compare to traditional alloying concepts? Please propose a hypothesis for their stability, identify relevant prior theoretical constraints, define the boundary conditions where these models might fail, and suggest an experiment to falsify the assumption of intrinsic stability.

generation.hypothesis: Nearly equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) will exhibit enhanced thermal stability and suppressed atomic diffusion compared to traditional alloys due to the synergistic effects of high configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion. Unlike traditional alloys where phase separation or precipitation is driven by thermodynamic instability, the high configurational entropy in HEA nanoparticles raises the free energy barrier for phase decomposition, while the severe lattice distortion impedes atomic diffusion (kinetic stabilization). However, at elevated temperatures, the high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles will introduce a competing driving force for surface energy minimization, potentially leading to Ostwald ripening or surface segregation, which may override the bulk stability mechanisms at very small sizes (<10 nm).
generation.material_initial_state: Nearly equiatomic quinary transition metal nanoparticles (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) in a chemically disordered face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution state, with particle sizes in the range of 5–50 nm.
generation.intervention: Heating the nanoparticles to elevated temperatures (e.g., 0.5–0.8 Tm, where Tm is the melting point) in an inert atmosphere or vacuum to induce thermal aging.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 300 K to 1200 K (depending on specific alloy Tm); Pressure: 1 atm (inert); Time: 1–100 hours; Particle size: 5–50 nm.
generation.structural_mediator: High configurational entropy (S_conf) and severe lattice distortion (Δr) acting as thermodynamic and kinetic barriers to phase separation and diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles and supported by partially transferring evidence (PMC6093928, PMC4999872). The high configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase solid solution by lowering the Gibbs free energy of the disordered state relative to ordered or segregated phases. Simultaneously, the severe lattice distortion caused by atomic size mismatch creates local strain fields that increase the activation energy for atomic diffusion, thereby kinetically suppressing precipitation and phase separation. However, in nanoparticles, the high surface energy acts as a driving force for coarsening (Ostwald ripening) and surface segregation, which may compete with the bulk stabilization mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nanoparticles will maintain their single-phase FCC structure and chemical homogeneity up to temperatures significantly higher than the onset of precipitation in bulk counterparts of the same composition. Atomic diffusion coefficients will be reduced by a factor of 2–10 compared to traditional alloys at the same temperature. However, for particles <10 nm, surface segregation of the most surface-active element (e.g., Ni or Mn) and Ostwald ripening will be observed, leading to a core-shell structure or particle coarsening, which represents a failure of the intrinsic stability model at the nanoscale.
generation.baseline: Traditional equiatomic alloys (e.g., binary or ternary) or bulk HEAs, which typically undergo phase separation, precipitation, or significant grain growth at temperatures >0.5 Tm due to lower configurational entropy and higher diffusion rates.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis of intrinsic stability fails when particle size drops below ~5 nm (where surface energy dominates) or when the temperature exceeds the solidus of the most volatile component, leading to evaporation or rapid surface segregation. Additionally, the presence of impurities or non-equimolar ratios may reduce the configurational entropy, lowering the stability threshold.
generation.uncertainty: High uncertainty regarding the exact threshold size for surface segregation dominance and the quantitative reduction in diffusion coefficients due to the lack of direct experimental data on diffusion in HEA nanoparticles. The interplay between magnetic fluctuations (relevant for CoCrFeMnNi) and thermal stability at elevated temperatures is also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize monodisperse CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles with controlled sizes (5, 10, 20, 50 nm). Heat them in an inert atmosphere at 0.6 Tm for 24 hours. Use in-situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to monitor structural and chemical evolution.
measurements: Particle size distribution (before and after heating)
Crystal structure (FCC vs. HCP vs. BCC)
Diffusion coefficients (via tracer diffusion or interdiffusion profiles)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles show significant phase separation (precipitation of ordered phases or secondary phases) or rapid coarsening (size increase >50%) within 24 hours at 0.6 Tm, or if the diffusion coefficients are found to be higher than those of traditional alloys, the hypothesis of intrinsic stability due to high configurational entropy and lattice distortion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials performance is central to the satisfactory operation of current and future nuclear energy systems due to the severe irradiation environment in reactors. Searching for structural materials with excellent irradiation tolerance is crucial for developing the next generation nuclear reactors. Here, we report the irradiation responses of a novel multi-component alloy system, high entropy alloy (HEA) Al x CoCrFeNi ( x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5), focusing on their precipitation behavior. It is found that the single phase system, Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi, exhibits a great phase stability against ion irradiation. No precipitate is observed even at the highest fluence. In contrast, numerous coherent precipitates are present in both multi-phase HEAs. Based on the irradiation-induced/enhanced precipitation theory, the excellent structural stability against precipitation of Al 0.1 CoCrFeNi is attributed to the high configurational entropy and low atomic diffusion, which reduces the thermodynamic driving force and kinetically restrains the formation of precipitate, respectively. It is well known that the high configurational entropies may stabilize solid solutions in equiatomic, multi-element HEAs. Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] .
